drills.title: A test with a PASS/FAIL line
drills.prompt: Arrange the lines into a tiny test program: the method under test, a check helper that compares expected with actual, and a main with two checks. Two lines do not belong.
lines: static double applyDiscount(double price, int percent) {
static void check(String name, double expected, double actual) {
drills.explain: A test calls the code with a known input and compares the result with the expected value written by hand. The helper plays the role of assertEquals(expected, actual): it prints PASS or FAIL for each check. == compares, a single = would assign (and not compile for a boolean test). The distractor formula (100 + percent) is the kind of bug a test like this exists to catch.
drills.output:
PASS ten percent off
PASS zero percent changes nothing

drills.title: Test that an error is thrown
drills.prompt: Fill the blanks so applyDiscount rejects a negative price, and the test checks both the exception type and its message. It should print PASS twice.
code: static double applyDiscount(double price, int percent) {
___ new IllegalArgumentException("Price must not be negative");
drills.explain: An error test has three parts: call the code that must fail, fail the test if nothing is thrown (the line after the call is only reached when no exception happened), and check the type and the message of what was caught. JUnit packs this into assertThrows. If the method threw a different exception type, the catch would not match and the program would crash, which also shows up as a failing test.

drills.title: Tests that depend on each other
drills.prompt: These checks share one static counter. Read the code and type exactly what it prints, one line per line of output.
drills.explain: items belongs to the class, so every check sees what the earlier ones left behind: the empty check fails because the first check already added 2, and the second run of the first check ends with 4. JUnit avoids this by creating a new test object for every @Test method and running @BeforeEach first, so each test starts from a fresh fixture. A test must pass or fail on its own, in any order.
drills.expected:
PASS two
FAIL empty, items=2
FAIL two, items=4

drills.title: The boundary the test caught
drills.prompt: Orders of Rs. 500 or more get free delivery. The program runs, but one check prints FAIL. Click the line of the code under test that is wrong, then choose the fix.
code: static void check(String name, boolean expected, boolean actual) {
check("big order is free", true, freeDelivery(900));
fixed_code: static void check(String name, boolean expected, boolean actual) {
check("big order is free", true, freeDelivery(900));

buggy_runs.output:
PASS small order pays
FAIL exactly 500 is free
PASS big order is free

drills.explain: "500 or more" is >=, and > leaves out exactly 500. The two checks far from the limit (120 and 900) pass either way, which is why a good test suite always includes a boundary check. Changing the boundary the other way (== or > 501) breaks a different check, and <= flips the whole rule.
drills.output:
PASS small order pays
PASS exactly 500 is free
PASS big order is free

drills.title: Review the AI's cart tests
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote these tests for a Cart class. They compile and run (all PASS), but tick the real problems with the tests (there are three).
code: static void check(String name, boolean ok) {
private final List<Integer> prices = new ArrayList<>();
int total() { int sum = 0; for (int p : prices) sum += p; return sum; }

issues.why: check("add works", true) passes whatever add does. A test needs a real assertion about a result, for example that total() is 20 after the add. A test that cannot fail gives false confidence.

issues.text: testText compares the whole toString() output character by character
issues.why: The test breaks when someone renames the currency, adds a space or reorders the text, although nothing is wrong. It checks the formatting, not the behaviour: assert on total() (or on the part that matters) instead.

issues.text: Only normal carts are tested: no empty cart, no zero or negative price
issues.why: Bugs live at the edges. A good test set also covers an empty cart (total 0), a boundary such as a price of 0 and the error case, so a wrong rule for negative prices would be noticed.

non_issues.text: Every test creates its own new Cart instead of sharing one
non_issues.why: That is the goal: each test starts from a fresh state and cannot be disturbed by the others. Sharing one cart would make the results depend on order.

non_issues.text: The expected value 35 is typed in instead of calculated from 20 and 15
non_issues.why: The expected value should be written by hand. Calculating it with the same logic as the code under test would repeat any bug in both places.

non_issues.text: main calls each test by hand instead of using a test runner
non_issues.why: For a small plain-Java demo this is fine. JUnit's @Test does the calling for you in real projects, but the checks themselves are the same.

drills.explain: Review tests as you review code: does every test have an assertion that can fail, does it check behaviour rather than formatting or internals, and do the cases cover normal, edge and error situations?
